title: The Mosque of Cordoba

lines: OUT OF THE SUN, INTO SHADE.
RED AND WHITE, RED AND WHITE.
cards: Step out of the hard southern sun, through a doorway, into shade. Your eyes take a moment. Then they find columns.
Rows of them, in every direction, slim stone trunks rising to arches.
And the arches are striped, red brick and pale stone, red and white, and above them a second tier of arches, as if the trees had grown branches on their branches. You can't see the end of it.
Wherever you stand, the rows open away from you. One word fits: a forest. This is the Mosque of Cordoba.

teach.b: It was begun under Abd al-Rahman, an Umayyad prince who had escaped to al-Andalus when his family lost power in the east.
Later rulers enlarged it again and again, keeping the same pattern each time, so the forest simply grew.
Historians say some of its columns were taken from older Roman and Visigothic buildings, so the stone itself has lived more than one life.

The double arches, by the usual explanation, were a builder's answer to a problem: the columns were short, and stacking arches lifted the roof high enough to let the hall breathe. Here's the thing to notice.
To the eye, the forest seems to go every way at once: no single center, no one view. But the people who prayed there didn't wander. Every row stood facing one wall, the qiblah wall.
And in that wall is the mihrab, a niche that shows worshippers which way to face, later covered with gold mosaic and carved stone. The Qur'an says the places of worship belong to God alone.
So a hall with endless paths had one direction built into it.
After Christian rulers took Cordoba, the building became a church, and later a cathedral was built up through the middle of the forest.
Today it serves as Cordoba's cathedral, and the arches still stand all around it. Visitors walk among them now.

how: In a mosque, a mihrab in the qiblah wall shows the direction of prayer toward Mecca, and the rows of worshippers stand facing it; the building in Cordoba is today a Catholic cathedral that visitors may tour.

games.why: later rulers enlarged it again and again, keeping the same pattern, which is why it reads as one forest.

practice: Picture yourself standing among the columns, the red and white stripes repeating around you, close, then farther, then farther still, your eye wandering down the rows for an end.

Then, gently, turn to face one way and stay there: let the forest stay wide while you stay pointed. If you pray, you can pray with your face turned one way; if not, just let your attention settle in one direction.

wordCard.voice: Mihrab. The niche in the qiblah wall of the Mosque of Cordoba, built by the Umayyads of al-Andalus, showing worshippers which way to face. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: the niche in a mosque's qiblah wall that marks the direction of prayer.
